entry.title: Real Analysis Appendix: Complex Fourier Series and Holomorphic Functions

link.title: Real Analysis Appendix: Complex Fourier Series and Holomorphic Functions

entry.content:
이 글은 2026년 봄학기 실변수함수론(MAT4033) 강의노트를 주제별로 정리한 글입니다.

During the Advanced Calculus course, we have studied Fourier series of the form as following definition.

Definition. Let \(\{\phi_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}\) be a sequence of orthogonal functions on \([a, b]\) and let \(f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]\). For each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), the number

\[c_n = \frac{\int_a^b f(x) \phi_n(x) dx}{\int_a^b \phi_n(x)^2 dx}\]

is called the Fourier coefficient of \(f\) with respect to \(\phi_n\). The series

\[f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} c_n \phi_n(x)\]

is called the Fourier series of \(f\).

Note that above definition of Fourier series is defined for any orthogonal system \(\{\phi_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}\). In particular, we usually use trigonometric system

\[\left\{1, \cos nx, \sin nx \right\}_{n=1}^{\infty},\]

which is orthogonal on \([-L, L]\). Now consider such trigonometric system on \([-\pi, \pi]\), we have

\[\int_{-\pi}^\pi \sin^{2} nx dx = \int_{-\pi}^\pi \cos^{2} n x dx = \pi, \quad \int_{-\pi}^\pi 1^{2} dx = 2\pi.\]

Therefore the Fourier coefficients of \(f\) with respect to the trigonometric system are defined as following:

Definition. Let \(f \in \mathcal{R}[-\pi, \pi]\). The Fourier coefficients of \(f\) with respect to the trigonometric system \(\{1, \cos nx, \sin nx\}\) are defined by

\[\begin{aligned} a_0 &= \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(x) dx, \\ a_n &= \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(x) \cos nx dx \qquad n = 1, 2, \ldots, \\ b_n &= \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(x) \sin nx dx \qquad n = 1, 2, \ldots. \end{aligned}\]

Also, the Fourier series of \(f\) is given by

\[f(x) \sim \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty (a_n \cos nx + b_n \sin nx).\]

For now, we want to extend such Fourier series to the complex form. By using Euler’s formula, we can rewrite the sine and cosine functions as

\[\begin{aligned} \cos nx &= \frac{e^{inx} + e^{-inx}}{2}, \\ \sin nx &= \frac{e^{inx} - e^{-inx}}{2i}. \end{aligned}\]

Then, we can express the Fourier series of \(f\) with above as

\[\begin{aligned} f(x) &\sim \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left( a_n \frac{e^{inx} + e^{-inx}}{2} + b_n \frac{e^{inx} - e^{-inx}}{2i} \right) \\ &= \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left( \frac{a_n - i b_n}{2} e^{inx} + \frac{a_n + i b_n}{2} e^{-inx} \right). \qquad (\ast)\\ \end{aligned}\]

Let define

\[c_0 \coloneq \frac{a_0}{2}, \quad c_n \coloneq \frac{a_n - i b_n}{2} \; \text{ for } n > 0, \quad \text{ and } \quad c_{-n} \coloneq \frac{a_n + i b_n}{2} \; \text{ for } n > 0.\]

Then,

\[(\ast) = c_0 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty c_n e^{inx} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty c_{-n} e^{-inx} = \sum_{n=-\infty}^\infty c_n e^{inx}.\]

Therefore, in general, we use the Fourier series of \(f\) in the complex form as following definition.

Definition. Let \(f \in \mathcal{R}[-\pi, \pi]\). The Fourier coefficients of \(f\) with respect to the complex trigonometric system \(\{e^{inx}\}_{n=-\infty}^\infty\) are defined by

\[c_n = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(x) e^{-inx} dx \quad \text{ for } n \in \mathbb{Z}.\]

Also, the Fourier series of \(f\) is given by

\[f(x) \sim \sum_{n=-\infty}^\infty c_n e^{inx}.\]

Holomorphic Functions

In the context of Complex Analysis, we are interested in functions of complex variable, which have much stronger properties than functions of a real variable. In particular, a function that is differentiable in the complex sense is infinitely differentiable and admits a power series expansion around every point in its domain. Such results have no direct analogue in real analysis, where many counterexamples arise.

entry.title: Real Analysis 17: Compact Operators
entry.content:
이 글은 2026년 봄학기 실변수함수론(MAT4033) 강의노트를 주제별로 정리한 글입니다.

Definition. A set \(X \subset H\) is compact if every sequence \(\{f_n\}\) in \(X\), there exists a subsequence \(\{f_{n_k}\}\) that converges in \(X\).

Remark.

  1. The closed ball \(B = \{f \in H : \vert \vert f\vert \vert \le r\} \subset H\) is compact if and only if \(\dim H < \infty\).

  2. In an infinite dimensional space, the orthonormal set \(\{e_n\}\) has no converging subsequence because \(\vert \vert e_n - e_m\vert \vert = \sqrt{2}\) for all \(n eq m\).

Definition. A linear operator \(T : H o H\) is compact if the closure of \(T(B) = \{T(f) : f \in B\}\) is compact.

Remark.

Equivalently, \(T\) is compact if every bounded sequence \(\{f_n\}\) in \(H\) has a subsequence \(\{f_{n_k}\}\) such that \(\{Tf_{n_k}\}\) converges.

Proposition 6.1.

Let \(T\) be a bounded linear operator on \(H\).

  1. If \(S\) is compact on \(H\), then so are \(ST\) and \(TS\).

  2. If \(\{T_n\}\) is a sequence of compact operators with \(\vert \vert T_n - T\vert \vert o 0\) as \(n o \infty\),

  3. If \(T\) is compact, then there exists a sequence of operators of finite rank such that \(\lim_{n o \infty} \vert \vert T_n - T\vert \vert = 0.\)

  4. \(T\) is compact if and only if \(T^*\) is compact.

Proof.

  1. Obvious.

  2. Let \(\{f_k\}\) be a bounded sequence in \(H\). Since \(T_1\) is compact, there exists a subsequence \(\{f_{1,k}\}\) of \(\{f_k\}\) such that \(\{T_1(f_{1,k})\}\) converges. We can find a further subsequence \(\{f_{2,k}\}\) such that \(\{T_2(f_{2,k})\}\) converges. Repeat this process. Let \(g_k = f_{k,k}\). Then, we find

    \[ egin{aligned} \vert \vert T(g_k) - T(g_l)\vert \vert &\le \vert \vert T(g_k) - T_m(g_k)\vert \vert + \vert \vert T_m(g_k) - T_m(g_l)\vert \vert + \vert \vert T_m(g_l) - T(g_l)\vert \vert \ &= I_1 + I_2 + I_3 \end{aligned}\]

    Since \(T_m o T\) and \(\{g_k\}\) is bounded, we find \(m\) large such that \(I_1, I_3 < rac{\epsilon}{3}\). With this fixed \(m\), we have \(I_2 < rac{\epsilon}{3}\) for sufficiently large \(k, l\). This implies \(\{T(g_k)\}\) is Cauchy in \(H\), and hence converges.

  3. Let \(\{e_k\}\) be a basis of \(H\). Let \(I = P_n + Q_n\), where \(P_n\) and \(Q_n\) are orthogonal projections onto \( ext{span}\{e_1, \dots, e_n\}\) and \( ext{span}\{e_{n+1}, \dots\}\) respectively. We claim that \(\vert \vert Q_n T\vert \vert o 0 \quad ext{as } n o \infty.\) If not, then there exists \(c > 0\) such that \(\vert \vert Q_n T\vert \vert \ge c \quad ext{ for all } n \in \mathbb{N},\) since \(\vert \vert Q_n g\vert \vert \searrow 0\) as \(n o \infty\) for all \(g \in H\).

    Hence, for each \(n\), there exists \(f_n\) with \(\vert \vert f_n\vert \vert = 1\) such that \(\vert \vert Q_n T f_n\vert \vert \ge c\). Since \(T\) is compact, there exists a subsequence such that \(Tf_{n_k} o g \quad ext{for some } g.\) But, since \(Q_{n_k}(g) = Q_{n_k} Tf_{n_k} - Q_{n_k}(Tf_{n_k} - g),\) we obtain

    \[\vert \vert Q_{n_k}(g)\vert \vert > rac{c}{2} \quad ext{for large } k.\]

    which is a contradiction.

  4. If \(T\) is compact, then \(\vert \vert T^* P_n - T^*\vert \vert = \vert \vert P_n T - T\vert \vert o 0.\) Since \(T^* P_n\) is of finite rank, \(T^*\) is compact by (ii).

Example (Hilbert-Schmidt process).

Let \(H = L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)\) and define \(T : H o H\) by

\[T(f)(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} K(x,y) f(y) dy\]

for some kernel \(K\). If \(K \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d imes \mathbb{R}^d)\), \(T\) is called a Hilbert-Schmidt operator.

Note that \(\vert \vert T\vert \vert \le \vert \vert K\vert \vert _{L^2(\mathbb{R}^d imes \mathbb{R}^d)}\), since

\[\vert T(f)(x)\vert \le \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \vert K(x,y)\vert \vert f(y)\vert dy \le \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \vert K(x,y)\vert ^2 dy ight)^{1/2} \vert \vert f\vert \vert _{L^2},\]

we obtain

\[\vert \vert Tf\vert \vert ^2 \le \int \left(\int \vert K(x,y)\vert ^2 dy ight) \vert \vert f\vert \vert ^2 dx = \vert \vert K\vert \vert _{L^2}^2 \vert \vert f\vert \vert ^2.\]

Now, consider an orthonormal basis \(\{\varphi_k\}\) for \(L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)\). Then \(\{\varphi_k(x) \varphi_l(y)\}_{k,l \ge 1}\) is an orthonormal basis for \(L^2(\mathbb{R}^d imes \mathbb{R}^d)\). Thus,

\[K(x,y) \sim \sum_{k,l} a_{kl} \varphi_k(x) \varphi_l(y) \quad ext{with } \sum_{k,l} \vert a_{kl}\vert ^2 < \infty.\]

We define

\[T_n(f)(x) \coloneq \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} K_n(x,y) f(y) dy\]

where \(K_n(x,y) \coloneq \sum_{k,l}^n a_{k,l} \varphi_k(x) \varphi_l(y).\) Then each \(T_n\) is compact. Moreover, since

\[\vert \vert K - K_n\vert \vert _{L^2(\mathbb{R}^d imes \mathbb{R}^d)}^2 = \sum_{\overset{k \ge n}{ ext{or} \; l \ge n}} \vert a_{k,l}\vert ^2 o 0,\]

we have \(\vert \vert T - T_n\vert \vert \le \vert \vert K - K_n\vert \vert o 0.\) Thus, \(T\) is compact by Proposition 6.1.

Theorem 6.2 (Spectral theorem).

Let \(T\) be a compact symmetric operator on \(H\). Then there exists an orthonormal basis \(\{\varphi_k\}\) of \(H\) that consists of eigenvectors of \(T\). That is,

\[T\varphi_k = \lambda_k \varphi_k\]

for some eigenvalue \(\lambda_k \in \mathbb{C}\).

Moreover, \(\lambda_k \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(\lambda_k o 0\) as \(k o \infty\). Conversely, every operator of this form is compact and symmetric.

Note that \(\{\lambda_k\}\) is called the spectrum of \(T\).

Lemma 6.3.

Let \(T\) be a bounded symmetric operator on \(H\).

  1. Every eigenvalue of \(T\) is real.

  2. If \(Tf_i = \lambda_i f_i\), \(i=1,2\) and \(\lambda_1 eq \lambda_2\), then \(f_1 \perp f_2\).

Proof.

  1. Let \(f\) be an eigenvector corresponding to \(\lambda\), then

    \[ egin{aligned} \lambda(f, f) &= (\lambda f, f) \ &= (Tf, f) \ &= (f, T^*f) \ &= (f, Tf) = (f, \lambda f) = \overline{\lambda}(f, f). \end{aligned}\]

    This implies that \(\lambda = \overline{\lambda} \implies \lambda \in \mathbb{R}\).

  2. Note that

    \[ egin{aligned} \lambda_1(f_1, f_2) &= (\lambda_1 f_1, f_2) \ &= (Tf_1, f_2) \ &= (f_1, T^*f_2) \ &= (f_1, Tf_2) \ &= (f_1, \lambda_2 f_2) = \lambda_2(f_1, f_2). \end{aligned}\]

    Since \(\lambda_1 eq \lambda_2\), we have \((f_1, f_2) = 0\).

Lemma 6.4.

Let \(T\) be a compact symmetric operator on \(H\).

  1. If \(\lambda eq 0\), the dimension of the null space of \(T - \lambda I\) is finite.

  2. There exists at most countable eigenvalues \(\{\lambda_k\}\) such that \(\lambda_k o 0\) as \(k o \infty\). <div class="real-analysis-footnote" markdown="1">Note: Equivalently, for all \(\mu > 0\), there exists \(N\) such that \(\vert \lambda_k\vert < \mu\) for all \(k \ge N\)</div>

Proof.

  1. Let \(V_\lambda = \ker(T - \lambda I)\). If \(\dim V_\lambda = \infty\), then there exists a sequence \(\{\varphi_n\}\) of orthonormal vectors in \(V_\lambda\).

    Since \(T\) is compact, there exists a subsequence \(\{\varphi_{n_k}\}\) such that \(T\varphi_{n_k}\) converges. This implies \(\lambda \varphi_{n_k}\) converges, which contradicts to \(\vert \vert \varphi_{n_k} - \varphi_{n_l}\vert \vert = \sqrt{2} \quad ext{for all } k eq l.\)

  2. Suppose to the contrary that for each \(\mu > 0\), there exists a sequence \(\{\lambda_n\}\) of distinct eigenvalues such that \(\vert \lambda_n\vert > \mu\).

    Let \(\varphi_n\) be corresponding eigenvector. By Lemma 6.3, \(\{\varphi_n\}\) is orthogonal. We may assume that \(\{\varphi_n\}\) is orthonormal. Since \(T\) is compact, there exists \(\{\varphi_{n_k}\}\) such that \(\{T\varphi_{n_k}\} = \{\lambda_{n_k}\varphi_{n_k}\} ext{ converges}.\) Then

    \[\vert \vert \lambda_{n_k}\varphi_{n_k} - \lambda_{n_l}\varphi_{n_l}\vert \vert ^2 = \lambda_{n_k}^2 + \lambda_{n_l}^2 > 2\mu^2 > 0,\]

    a contradiction.

Lemma 6.5.

Suppose \(T eq 0\) is compact and symmetric. Then either \(\vert \vert T\vert \vert\) or \(-\vert \vert T\vert \vert\) is an eigenvalue of \(T\).

Proof. Recall that \(\vert \vert T\vert \vert = \sup \{\vert (Tf, f)\vert : \vert \vert f\vert \vert = 1\}.\)

Since \(T\) is symmetric, we have either

\[\vert \vert T\vert \vert = \sup \{(Tf, f) : \vert \vert f\vert \vert = 1\} ext{ or } -\vert \vert T\vert \vert = \inf \{(Tf, f) : \vert \vert f\vert \vert = 1\}\]

Assume the first case, and \(\lambda = \vert \vert T\vert \vert\). Then there exists \(\{f_n\} \subset H\) such that \(\vert \vert f_n\vert \vert = 1\) and \((Tf_n, f_n) o \lambda\). Since \(T\) is compact, there exists \(\{f_{n_k}\}\) such that \(Tf_{n_k} o g \in H\) as \(k o \infty\). Then

\[ egin{aligned} \vert \vert Tf_{n_k} - \lambda f_{n_k}\vert \vert ^2 &= \vert \vert Tf_{n_k}\vert \vert ^2 - 2\lambda(Tf_{n_k}, f_{n_k}) + \lambda^2 \vert \vert f_{n_k}\vert \vert ^2 \ &\le \lambda^2 - 2\lambda(Tf_{n_k}, f_{n_k}) + \lambda^2 o 0 \quad ext{as } k o \infty. \end{aligned}\]

Thus, \(\lambda f_{n_k} o g\). Since \(T\) is continuous, we have

\[T(\lambda f_{n_k}) = \lambda T(f_{n_k}) \longrightarrow Tg = \lambda g.\]

If \(g = 0\), we get \(\lambda = \lim_{k o \infty} (Tf_{n_k}, f_{n_k}) = 0\) which implies that \(\vert \vert T\vert \vert = 0 \implies T = 0\), a contradiction to \(T eq 0\).

Therefore, \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of \(T\).

Proof of Theorem 6.2.

Let \(S = \overline{ ext{span} \{ ext{eigenvectors of } T \}}\). Then \(S eq \{0\}\), by Lemma 6.5.

If \(S = H\), then we are done.

Otherwise, \(H = S \oplus S^\perp\) with \(S^\perp eq \{0\}\). Note that \(f \in S \implies Tf \in S\) and \(g \in S^\perp \implies Tg \in S^\perp\) since \((Tg, h) = (g, Th) = 0\) for all \(h \in S\).

Now consider the projection \(T_1 : S^\perp o S^\perp\). It is straightforward to check that \(T_1\) is compact and symmetric.

Since \(T_1 eq 0\), it follows from Lemma 6.5 that \(T_1\) has a nonzero eigenvector in \(S^\perp\). This is also an eigenvector of \(T\).

entry.title: Real Analysis 16: Linear Transformations and the Riesz Representation Theorem

link.title: Real Analysis 16: Linear Transformations and the Riesz Representation Theorem

entry.content:
이 글은 2026년 봄학기 실변수함수론(MAT4033) 강의노트를 주제별로 정리한 글입니다.

Definition.

  1. A mapping \(T : H_1 o H_2\) is linear if \(T(af + bg) = aT(f) + bT(g)\) for all \(a, b \in \mathbb{C}\) and \(f, g \in H_1\).

  2. A linear operator \(T\) is bounded if there exists \(M < \infty\) such that \(\vert \vert T(f)\vert \vert _{H_2} \le M \vert \vert f\vert \vert _{H_1} ext{ for all } f \in H_1.\)

  3. The norm of \(T \coloneq \vert \vert T\vert \vert \coloneq \inf M \ge 0\).

  4. A linear operator \(T\) is continuous if \(T(f_n) o T(f)\) whenever \(f_n o f\).

Lemma 5.1.

\(\vert \vert T\vert \vert = \sup \left\{ \vert (Tf, g)\vert : \vert \vert f\vert \vert , \vert \vert g\vert \vert \le 1 ight\}\).

Proof. (\(\ge\)) If \(\vert \vert T\vert \vert \le M\), the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives \(\vert (Tf, g)\vert \le \vert \vert Tf\vert \vert \vert \vert g\vert \vert \le M\) whenever \(\vert \vert f\vert \vert \le 1\) and \(\vert \vert g\vert \vert \le 1\). Hence,

\[\vert \vert Tf\vert \vert \vert \vert g\vert \vert \le M \implies \vert \vert Tf\vert \vert \vert \vert g\vert \vert \le \inf M = \vert \vert T\vert \vert .\]

Taking the infimum over \(M\) gives the inequality (\(\ge\)).

(\(\le\)) Suppose the right-hand side \(\le M\). ETS : \(\vert \vert Tf\vert \vert \le M\vert \vert f\vert \vert\) for all \(f\)

  1. If \(f = 0\), there is nothing to prove.

  2. If \(f eq 0\), we take

    \[f' = rac{f}{\vert \vert f\vert \vert } ext{ and } g' = rac{Tf}{\vert \vert Tf\vert \vert }.\]

    Since \(\vert \vert f'\vert \vert = \vert \vert g'\vert \vert = 1\), we have

    \[M \ge \vert (Tf', g')\vert = rac{1}{\vert \vert f\vert \vert \vert \vert Tf\vert \vert } \vert (Tf, Tf)\vert = rac{\vert \vert Tf\vert \vert }{\vert \vert f\vert \vert }.\]

Proposition 5.2.

A linear operator \(T : H_1 o H_2\) is bounded if and only if it is continuous.

Proof. (\(\implies\)) is clear since \(\vert \vert Tf - Tf_n\vert \vert \le M \vert \vert f - f_n\vert \vert\).

(\(\impliedby\)) If \(T\) is continuous, but not bounded, then for each \(n\), there exists \(f_n eq 0\) such that \(\vert \vert Tf_n\vert \vert \ge n \vert \vert f_n\vert \vert\). Let \(g_n = rac{f_n}{n \vert \vert f_n\vert \vert }, ext{ then } \vert \vert g_n\vert \vert = rac{1}{n} o 0 ext{ as } n o \infty.\) Since \(T\) is continuous, \(T(g_n) o 0\) which contradicts \(\vert \vert Tg_n\vert \vert \ge 1\).<div class="real-analysis-footnote" markdown="1">Note: Since \(Tg_n = rac{Tf_n}{n\vert \vert f_n\vert \vert } \implies \vert \vert Tg_n\vert \vert = rac{\vert \vert Tf_n\vert \vert }{n\vert \vert f_n\vert \vert } \ge 1\)</div>

Remark.

Any linear operator between finite dimensional Hilbert spaces is continuous.

4.5.1 Linear functionals and the Riesz representation theorem

Definition. A linear operator \(l : H o \mathbb{C}\) is called a linear functional.

Theorem 5.3 (Riesz).

If \(l\) is a continuous linear functional, then there exists \(g \in H\) such that \(l(f) = (f, g)\) for all \(f \in H\). Moreover, \(\vert \vert l\vert \vert = \vert \vert g\vert \vert _{H}\)

Proof. The so-called null space \(S = \{f \in H : l(f) = 0\}\) of \(l\) is a closed subspace of \(H\), since \(l\) is continuous.

  1. If \(S = H\), then \(l = 0\) and we take \(g = 0\).

  2. Suppose \(S eq H\). <div class="real-analysis-footnote" markdown="1">Note: Idea of the proof: If \(f = f_1 + f_2 \in S \oplus S^\perp\), then \(l(f) = (f, g) \iff l(f_1) + l(f_2) = (f_1, g) + (f_2, g).\) Note that \(l(f_1) = 0\). Since \(l(f_1) + l(f_2)\) is independent of \(f_1\), we must have \((f_1, g) = 0.\) That is, we must look for \(g\) in \(S^\perp\).</div> We take \(0 eq h \in S^\perp\). Since \(u \coloneq l(f)h - l(h)f \in S = \ker l\) we have \(0 = (u, h) = l(f)(h, h) - l(h)(f, h).\) Thus,

    \[g \coloneq rac{\overline{l(h)}}{\vert \vert h\vert \vert ^2} h \quad ext{ gives } \quad l(f) = (f, g).\]

    Note: \(l(f)h - l(h)f \in S = \ker l\) since \(l(l(f)h - l(h)f) = l(f)l(h) - l(h)l(f) = 0.\) Last equality comes from

    \[ egin{aligned} l(f)(h,h) - l(h)(f,h) = 0 &\implies l(f)\vert \vert h\vert \vert ^2 = l(h)(f,h) \ &\implies l(f) = rac{l(h)}{\vert \vert h\vert \vert ^2}(f, h) = \left(f, rac{\overline{l(h)}}{\vert \vert h\vert \vert ^2} h ight) \end{aligned}\]

4.5.2 Adjoints

Proposition 5.4.

Let \(T : H o H\) be a bounded linear transformation. Then there exists a unique bounded linear transformation \(T^*\) on \(H\) such that

  1. \((Tf, g) = (f, T^*g)\)

  2. \(\vert \vert T\vert \vert = \vert \vert T^*\vert \vert\)

  3. \[(T^*)^* = T\]

\(T^*\) is called the adjoint of \(T\).

Proof. For each fixed \(g \in H\), define the linear functional \(l : H o \mathbb{C}\) by \(l(f) = (Tf, g).\) Then,

\[ egin{aligned} \vert l(f)\vert = \vert (Tf, g)\vert &\le \vert \vert Tf\vert \vert \vert \vert g\vert \vert \ &\le (\vert \vert T\vert \vert \vert \vert g\vert \vert ) \vert \vert f\vert \vert . \end{aligned}\]

that is, \(l\) is bounded. Thus, by the Riesz representation theorem, there exists a unique \(h = h_g \in H\) such that \(l(f) = (f, h)\). We define \(T^* : H o H\) by \(T^*g = h\). Hence, (i) is clear.

Also,

\[ egin{aligned} \vert \vert T\vert \vert &= \sup \{\vert (Tf, g)\vert : \vert \vert f\vert \vert , \vert \vert g\vert \vert \le 1\} \ &= \sup \{\vert (f, T^*g)\vert : \vert \vert f\vert \vert , \vert \vert g\vert \vert \le 1\} = \vert \vert T^*\vert \vert \end{aligned}\]

This gives (ii). Finally, we have \((T^*f, g) = \overline{(g, T^*f)} = \overline{(Tg, f)} = (f, Tg)\) This implies \((T^*)^* = T\).

Definition. A linear operator \(T\) is symmetric, hermitian or self-adjoint if \(T = T^*\).

Remark.

If \(T = T^*\), then \(\vert \vert T\vert \vert = \sup \{\vert (Tf, f)\vert : \vert \vert f\vert \vert = 1\}.\) Indeed, by Lemma 5.1, \(\vert \vert T\vert \vert = \sup \{\vert (Tf, g)\vert : \vert \vert f\vert \vert , \vert \vert g\vert \vert \le 1\}\). Thus, (\(\ge\)) is clear.

이 글은 2026년 봄학기 실변수함수론(MAT4033) 강의노트를 주제별로 정리한 글입니다.

Definition. A subspace \(S\) of Hilbert space \(H\) is closed if whenever \(\{f_n\} \subset S\) converges to \(f \in H\), then \(f\) also belongs to \(S\).

Remark.

  1. If \(\vert H\vert < \infty\), then any subspace is closed.

  2. If \(\vert H\vert = \infty\), this is not true in general: \(\mathbb{R} \le L^2\) is not closed.

Lemma 4.1.

Let \(S \le H\)<div class="real-analysis-footnote" markdown="1">Note: We will denote subspace \(S\) of \(H\) by \(S \le H\).</div> be closed and \(f \in H\).

  1. There exsits \(g_0 \in S\) uniquely such that \(\vert \vert f - g_0\vert \vert = \inf_{g \in S} \vert \vert f - g\vert \vert\)

  2. \(f - g_0 \perp S\), that is, \((f - g_0 \: , \: g) = 0\) for all \(g \in S\)

Proof.

  1. Let \(d = \inf_{g \in S} \vert \vert f - g\vert \vert\). Since \(f \notin S\) and \(S\) is closed, \(d > 0\). Then we can choose a sequence \(\{g_n\}\) such that \(\vert \vert f - g_n\vert \vert \to d\) as \(n \to \infty\). Then, ETS : \(\{g_n\}\) is Cauchy in \(H\). We use following equality: for all \(A, B \in H\),

    \[\vert \vert A + B\vert \vert ^2 + \vert \vert A - B\vert \vert ^2 = 2(\vert \vert A\vert \vert ^2 + \vert \vert B\vert \vert ^2)\]

    Applying it to \(A = f - g_n\) \& \(B = f - g_m\), we find

    \[\begin{aligned} \vert \vert g_n - g_m\vert \vert ^2 &= 2(\vert \vert f - g_n\vert \vert ^2 + \vert \vert f - g_m\vert \vert ^2) - \vert \vert 2f - g_n - g_m\vert \vert ^2 \\ &\le 2(\vert \vert f - g_n\vert \vert ^2 + \vert \vert f - g_m\vert \vert ^2) - (2d)^2 \qquad (\ast) \end{aligned}\]

    then, \((\ast)\to 2(d^2 + d^2) - 4d^2 = 0 \quad \text{as } n, m \to \infty\).

    Uniqueness follows from (ii): If \(\tilde{g}_0\) is another minimizer, then

    \[(f - g_0) \perp (g_0 - \tilde{g}_0)\]

    Hence, \(\vert \vert f - \tilde{g}_0\vert \vert ^2 = \vert \vert f - g_0\vert \vert ^2 + \vert \vert g_0 - \tilde{g}_0\vert \vert ^2\).

  2. Let \(g \in S\) and \(\epsilon \in \mathbb{R}\). Since \(g_0 - \epsilon g \in S\), we have

    Note: Following inequality comes from the following calculation:

    \[\begin{aligned} \vert \vert f - g_0 + \epsilon g\vert \vert ^2 &= \langle f - g_0 + \epsilon g, f - g_0 + \epsilon g \rangle \\ &= \langle f - g_0, f - g_0 \rangle + \langle f - g_0, \epsilon g \rangle + \langle \epsilon g, f - g_0 \rangle + \langle \epsilon g, \epsilon g \rangle \\ &= \vert \vert f - g_0\vert \vert ^2 + \vert \vert \epsilon g\vert \vert ^2 + \langle f - g_0, \epsilon g \rangle + \langle \epsilon g, f - g_0 \rangle, \end{aligned}\]

    and since

    \[\begin{aligned} \langle f - g_0, \epsilon g \rangle + \langle \epsilon g, f - g_0 \rangle &= \epsilon \langle f - g_0, g \rangle + \epsilon \overline{\langle f - g_0, g \rangle} \\ &= 2\epsilon \text{Re} \langle f - g_0, g \rangle \\ \end{aligned}\]
    \[\begin{aligned} \vert \vert f - g_0\vert \vert ^2 &\le \vert \vert f - (g_0 - \epsilon g)\vert \vert ^2 \\ &= \vert \vert f - g_0\vert \vert ^2 + \epsilon^2 \vert \vert g\vert \vert ^2 + 2\epsilon \text{Re}(f - g_0, g) \qquad (\ast) \end{aligned}\]

    Then, \(\text{Re} \langle f - g_0, g \rangle = 0\). Indeed,

    1. if \(\text{Re} \langle f - g_0, g \rangle > 0\), then we can take sufficiently small \(\epsilon > 0\) such that \(\epsilon^2 \vert \vert g\vert \vert ^2 \le 2\epsilon \text{Re} \langle f - g_0, g \rangle,\) which is a contradiction.

    2. if \(\text{Re} \langle f - g_0, g \rangle < 0\), again, take small \(\epsilon < 0\) so that \(\epsilon^2 \vert \vert g\vert \vert ^2 \le 2\epsilon \text{Re} \langle f - g_0, g \rangle.\) Thus, \(\text{Re} \langle f - g_0, g \rangle = 0\).

    Similarly, by considering \(g_0 - i\epsilon g\), we obtain \(\text{Im}(f - g_0, g) = 0\). Thus, \((f - g_0, g) = 0\).

Definition. The orthogonal complement of \(S \le H\) is defined by

\[S^\perp = \{f \in H : (f, g) = 0 \text{ for all } g \in S\}.\]

Remark.

\(S^\perp \le H\), \(S \cap S^\perp = \{0\}\) and \(S^\perp\) is closed. (Proof is homework).RT

Proposition 4.2.

If \(S \le H\) is closed, then \(H = S \oplus S^\perp \text{ (direct sum)}.\) That is, \(f \in H\) can be written uniquely as \(f = g + h\), where \(g \in S\) and \(h \in S^\perp\).

Proof. For \(f \in H\), we take \(g_0\) as in Lemma 4.1, and write \(f = g_0 + (f - g_0).\) Then \(g_0 \in S\) and \(f - g_0 \in S^\perp\). For the uniqueness, assume \(f = g_1 + h_1 = g_2 + h_2\) where \(g_i \in S\), \(h_i \in S^\perp\). Then, \(g_1 - g_2 = h_2 - h_1 \in S \cap S^\perp = \{0\}.\) Thus, \(g_1 = g_2\) and \(h_1 = h_2\).

Definition. The map \(P_S(f) = g_0\) is called the (orthogonal) projection onto \(S\).

Example 1.

On \(L^2[-\pi, \pi]\), the partial sum operator \(S_N(f) \coloneq \sum_{n=-N}^N a_n e^{in\theta}\) of the Fourier Series is the projection onto the closed subspace \(\text{span}\{e^{-iN\theta}, \dots, e^{iN\theta}\}.\) That is, \(S_N : L^2 \to \text{span}\{e^{-iN\theta}, \dots, e^{iN\theta}\}\).

Example 2.

Let \(S\) denote the subspace of \(L^2[-\pi, \pi]\) that consists of all \(F\) with \(F(\theta) \sim \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n e^{in\theta} \text{ where n < 0 \implies a_n = 0 }\) By Fatou’s theorem, \(S\) can be identified with the Hardy space \(H^2(\mathbb{D})\). Then the projection from \(L^2\) to \(S\) can be written as

\[\begin{aligned} P(f)(z) &= \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n z^n \\ &= \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left( \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(e^{i\theta}) e^{-in\theta} d\theta \right) z^n \end{aligned}\]

Note that for \(f \in L^1\):

\[\begin{aligned} P(f)(z) &= \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(e^{i\theta}) \sum_{n=0}^\infty (e^{-i\theta} z)^n d\theta \qquad (\because f \in L^1, \text{ by DCT})\\ &= \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi \frac{f(e^{i\theta})}{1 - e^{-i\theta} z} d\theta \\ &= \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{-\pi}^\pi \frac{f(e^{i\theta})}{e^{i\theta} - z} i e^{i\theta} d\theta \\ &= \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_\gamma \frac{f(\zeta)}{\zeta - z} d\zeta \quad (d\zeta = i e^{i\theta} d\theta) \\ &\coloneq \text{Cauchy integral of } f \text{ along } \gamma = \text{unit circle}. \end{aligned}\]

Exercise: 10, 11, 12.

entry.title: Real Analysis 14: Fourier Series and Fatou’s Theorem

link.title: Real Analysis 14: Fourier Series and Fatou’s Theorem

entry.content:
이 글은 2026년 봄학기 실변수함수론(MAT4033) 강의노트를 주제별로 정리한 글입니다.

Definition. For \(f \in L^1[-\pi, \pi]\), we define the Fourier series of \(f\) by

\[f(x) \sim \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a_n e^{inx}, \quad ext{where} \quad a_n \coloneq rac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(x) e^{-inx} dx.\]

Theorem 3.2.

Let \(f \in L^2[-\pi, \pi] (\subset L^1[-\pi, \pi])\). Then

  1. (Parseval’s identity)

    \[\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \vert a_n\vert ^2 = rac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi \vert f\vert ^2\]

  2. The mapping \(L^2[-\pi, \pi] o l^2(\mathbb{Z})\) which maps \(f \mapsto \{a_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}\) is a unitary map.

  3. The Fourier series of \(f\) converges to \(f\) in \(L^2\), that is,

    \[ rac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi \vert f(x) - S_N(f)\vert ^2 dx o 0 \quad ext{as } N o \infty\]

    where \(S_N(f) = \sum_{\vert n\vert \le N} a_n e^{inx}\).

Proof. Apply Theorem 2.3 to \(H = L^2[-\pi, \pi]\) with the usual inner product and the orthonormal set \(\{e^{inx}\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}\).

Remark.

For \(L^1\) function \(f\), the Fourier series may diverge everywhere.

Theorem 3.1.

Let \(f \in L^1[-\pi, \pi]\).

  1. If \(a_n = 0\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\), then \(f = 0\) a.e.

  2. \(\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a_n r^{\vert n\vert } e^{inx} o f(x)\) for a.e. \(x\) as \(r earrow 1\).

Remark.

Since

\[\sum \vert a_n r^{\vert n\vert } e^{inx}\vert \le \left( rac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi \vert f(x)\vert dx ight) \sum r^{\vert n\vert }\]

the series \(\sum a_n r^{\vert n\vert } e^{inx}\) converges absolutely and uniformly (in \(x\)) for each \(r \in [0, 1)\).

Proof. ETS : (ii) holds, since (i) follows from (ii).

A straightforward calculation shows that

\[\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} r^{\vert n\vert } e^{iny} = rac{1 - r^2}{1 - 2r \cos y + r^2} \eqcolon Pr(y) \qquad ext{(Poisson kernel)}\]

We extend \(f\) as the \(2\pi\)-periodic function on \(\mathbb{R}\). We claim that

\[\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a_n r^{\vert n\vert } e^{inx} = rac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(x-y) P_r(y) dy.\]

Indeed, by the DCT,

\[ egin{aligned} RHS &= \sum r^{\vert n\vert } rac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(x-y) e^{iny} dy \ &= \sum r^{\vert n\vert } rac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi+x}^{\pi+x} f(y) e^{in(x-y)} dy \ &= \sum r^{\vert n\vert } e^{inx} rac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(y) e^{-iny} dy = LHS \end{aligned}\]

Note that \(RHS o f(x)\) at every Lebesgue point of \(f\) as \(r earrow 1\).

4.3.1 Fatou’s theorem

Question.

Let \(F(z)\) be holomorphic in

\[D = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : \vert z\vert < 1\}\]

What are conditions on \(F\) that guarantee that \(F(z)\) will converge, in an appropriate sense, to boundary values

\[F(e^{i heta}) ext{ on } \partial D?\]

Please see also Exercise 16.

Theorem 3.3 (Fatou).

A bounded holomorphic function \(F(re^{i heta})\) on \(D\) has radial limits

\[\lim_{r earrow 1} F(re^{i heta})\]

exists for almost every \( heta\).

Proof. Recall that \(F(z)\) has a power series expansion \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n z^n\) in \(D\) that converges absolutely and uniformly in every compact subset of \(D\). Thus, we have

\[ egin{aligned} rac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi F(re^{i heta}) e^{-ik heta} d heta &= rac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n (re^{i heta})^n e^{-ik heta} d heta \ &= \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n r^n rac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi e^{i(n-k) heta} d heta = egin{cases} a_k r^k & ext{if } k \ge 0 \ 0 & ext{if } k < 0 \end{cases} \end{aligned}\]

Since \(F(re^{i heta}) \in L^2[-\pi, \pi]\) for each \(0 \le r < 1\), we can apply Parseval’s identity:

\[\sum_{n=0}^\infty \vert a_n\vert ^2 r^{2n} = rac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi \vert F(re^{i heta})\vert ^2 d heta \quad ext{ for each } r \in (0, 1).\]

By the boundedness of \(F\), letting \(r earrow 1\) shows that \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty \vert a_n\vert ^2\) converges.

Now, we define \(F(e^{i heta})\) by the \(L^2\) function where Fourier coefficients are \(a_n\) when \(n \ge 0\), and \(0\) when \(n < 0\).<div class="real-analysis-footnote" markdown="1">Note: Existence and uniqueness of such \(L^2\)-function, under the assumption \(\{a_n\} \in l^2\), by the Riesz-Fischer theorem.</div> Hence by Theorem 3.1 (ii),

\[F(re^{i heta}) \coloneq \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n r^n e^{in heta} o F(e^{i heta})\]

for a.e. \( heta\) as \(r earrow 1\).

Remark.

What we need in the proof is finiteness of

\[\sup_{0 \le r < 1} rac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi \vert F(re^{i heta})\vert ^2 d heta < \infty\]

which is weaker than the boundedness. Theorem 3.3 holds for any function in the Hardy space

\[H^2(\mathbb{D}) = \left\{ F : \mathbb{D} o \mathbb{C} ext{ holomorphic} : \sup_{0 \le r < 1} rac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi \vert F(re^{i heta})\vert ^2 d heta < \infty ight\}.\]

entry.title: Real Analysis 13: Hilbert Spaces—Orthogonality and Unitary Mappings

link.title: Real Analysis 13: Hilbert Spaces—Orthogonality and Unitary Mappings

entry.content:
이 글은 2026년 봄학기 실변수함수론(MAT4033) 강의노트를 주제별로 정리한 글입니다.

Hilbert space.

An inner product space is called a Hilbert space if it is complete and separable.

Note: Some textbook defines a Hilbert space without the separability condition. Indeed, for advanced and modern mathemathics, this is more usual but quiet difficult to prove its properties. In this course, we will add the separability condition. See the Problem 2 for a non-separable example.</div>

Example 1.

Let \(E \in \mathcal{M}\) be with \(m(E) > 0\). Define \(L^2(E)\) by the space of square integrable functions \(f : E \to \mathbb{C}\) such that

\[\vert \vert f\vert \vert _{L^2(E)} \coloneq \left(\int_E \vert f\vert ^2\right)^{1/2} < \infty.\]

Being equipped with the inner product

\[(f, g) \coloneq \int_E f \overline{g}\]

\(L^2(E)\) becomes a Hilbert space.

Example 2.

\(\mathbb{R}^N\) and \(\mathbb{C}^N\) with the usual inner product

\[(a, b) \coloneq \sum_{k=1}^N a_k \overline{b}_k\]

where \(a = (a_1, \dots, a_N)\) and \(b = (b_1, \dots, b_N)\) are Hilbert space.

Example 3.

The space

\[l^2(\mathbb{Z}) \coloneq \left\{ (a_n)_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} : a_n \in \mathbb{C}, \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \vert a_n\vert ^2 < \infty \right\}\]

with the inner product

\[(a, b) \coloneq \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a_n \overline{b}_n\]

is a Hilbert space. (See Exercise 4).

Similarly, \(l^2(\mathbb{N})\) is also a Hilbert space which is given by

\[l^2(\mathbb{N}) \coloneq \left\{ (a_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} : a_n \in \mathbb{C}, \sum_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \vert a_n\vert ^2 < \infty \right\}\]

with the inner product

\[(a, b) \coloneq \sum_{n \in \mathbb{N}} a_n \overline{b}_n.\]

4.2.1 Orthogonality

Definition. Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space.

  1. \(f, g \in H\) are orthogonal or perpendicular and write \(f \perp g\) if \((f, g) = 0\).

  2. At most countable subset \(\{e_k\} \subset H\) is orthonormal if \((e_i, e_j) = \delta_{ij}\).

Proposition 2.1.

If \(f \perp g\), then \(\vert \vert f + g\vert \vert ^2 = \vert \vert f\vert \vert ^2 + \vert \vert g\vert \vert ^2\).

Proof. \(\vert \vert f + g\vert \vert ^2 = \vert \vert f\vert \vert ^2 + (f, g) + (g, f) + \vert \vert g\vert \vert ^2 = \vert \vert f\vert \vert ^2 + \vert \vert g\vert \vert ^2\).

Proposition 2.2.

If \(\{e_k\}_{k=1}^\infty\) is orthonormal and \(f = \sum a_k e_k\) is a finite sum, then

\[\vert \vert f\vert \vert ^2 = \sum \vert a_k\vert ^2.\]

Definition. An orthonormal set \(\{e_k\}\) is called an orthonormal basis for \(H\), if \(\text{span}\{e_k\}\) is dense in \(H\).

Theorem 2.3.

Let \(\{e_k\}\) be orthonormal. The followings are equivalent:

  1. \(\{e_k\}\) is an orthonormal basis for \(H\).

  2. If \(f \in H\) and \((f, e_j) = 0\) for all \(j\), then \(f = 0\).

  3. If \(f \in H\) and \(S_N(f) \coloneq \sum_{k=1}^N a_k e_k\) where \(a_k = (f, e_k)\), then \(\lim_{N \to \infty} S_N(f) = f\).

  4. (Parseval’s identity). If \(a_k = (f, e_k)\), then \(\vert \vert f\vert \vert ^2 = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \vert a_k\vert ^2\).

Proof. (i) \(\implies\) (ii).
There exists \(\{g_n\} \subset \text{span}\{e_k\}\) such that

\[\vert \vert f - g_n\vert \vert \to 0 \text{ as } n \to \infty\]

Since \((f, e_j) = 0\) for all \(j\), we have

\[(f, g_n) = 0 \quad \text{for all } n.\]

By Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,

\[\vert \vert f\vert \vert ^2 = (f, f) = (f, f - g_n) \le \vert \vert f\vert \vert \vert \vert f - g_n\vert \vert \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.\]

Thus, \(f = 0\).
(ii) \(\implies\) (iii).

  1. We have

    \[\begin{aligned} (f - S_N(f), S_N(f)) &= (f, S_N(f)) - \vert \vert S_N(f)\vert \vert ^2 \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^N a_k(f, e_k) - \sum_{k=1}^N \vert a_k\vert ^2 = 0. \end{aligned}\]

    Thus,

    \[\begin{aligned} \vert \vert f\vert \vert ^2 &= \vert \vert f - S_N(f)\vert \vert ^2 + \vert \vert S_N(f)\vert \vert ^2 \\ &\ge \sum_{k=1}^N \vert a_k\vert ^2 \qquad (\because Bessel's inequality) \end{aligned}\]

    since \(\vert \vert f - S_N(f)\vert \vert ^2 \ge 0\) and \(\vert \vert S_N(f)\vert \vert ^2 = \sum_{k=1}^N \vert a_k\vert ^2\). This implies that \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty \vert a_k\vert ^2\) converges. Since

    \[\vert \vert S_N(f) - S_M(f)\vert \vert ^2 = \sum_{k=M+1}^N \vert a_k\vert ^2\]

    whenever \(N > M\), \(\{S_N(f)\}\) is Cauchy in \(H\), and hence \(S_N(f) \to g\) for some \(g \in H\).

  2. For a fixed \(j\), we have

    \[(f - S_N(f), e_j) = a_j - a_j = 0\]

    for \(N \ge j\). Since \(S_N(f) \to g\), we can conclude

    \[(f - g, e_j) = 0 \quad \text{for all } j.\]

    By (ii), \(f = g = \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k e_k\).

(iii) \(\implies\) (iv).
Note that

\[\begin{aligned} \vert \vert f\vert \vert ^2 &= \vert \vert f - S_N(f)\vert \vert ^2 + \vert \vert S_N(f)\vert \vert ^2 \\ &= \vert \vert f - S_N(f)\vert \vert ^2 + \sum_{k=1}^N \vert a_k\vert ^2. \qquad (\ast) \end{aligned}\]

By taking \(N \to \infty\) in \((\ast)\), we obtain \(\vert \vert f\vert \vert ^2 = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \vert a_k\vert ^2.\)

(iv) \(\implies\) (i).
Again from \((\ast)\),

\[\vert \vert f - S_N(f)\vert \vert \to 0 \text{ as } N \to \infty,\]

i.e. \(\text{span}\{e_k\}\) is dense in \(H\).

Linear independence.

A countable set \(\{e_k\}\) is linearly independent if all finite subsets are linearly independent.

Theorem 2.4.

Any Hilbert space \(H\) has an orthonormal basis.

Proof. Since \(H\) is separable, there exists a countable collection of \(\mathcal{F} = \{f_k\}\) in \(H\) such that

\[\text{span}\{\mathcal{F}_k\} \text{ is dense in } H.\]

We may assume \(\{f_k\}\) is linearly independent.

  1. If \(\mathcal{F}\) is finite, then the Gram-Schmidt process yields an orthonormal basis. In this case, \(H\) is said to be finite-dimensional. Otherwise, it is infinite-dimensional.

  2. If \(\mathcal{F}\) is infinite, we prove by induction that there exists an orthonormal set \(\{e_k\}\) such that

    \[\text{span}\{e_1, \dots, e_n\} = \text{span}\{f_1, \dots, f_n\} \qquad (\ast\ast)\]

    for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). We first take

    \[e_1 = \frac{f_1}{\vert \vert f_1\vert \vert }\]

    Next, assume that we have found \(e_1, \dots, e_k\) such that \((\ast\ast)\) holds for \(n = k\). Then,

    \[e_{k+1}' = f_{k+1} - \sum_{j=1}^k a_j e_j\]

    with \(a_j = (f_{k+1}, e_j)\) is orthogonal to \(\{e_1, \dots, e_k\}\). Let

    \[e_{k+1} = \frac{e_{k+1}'}{\vert \vert e_{k+1}'\vert \vert }\]

    Then, \(\{e_1, \dots, e_{k+1}\}\) is orthonormal and \((\ast\ast)\) holds for \(n = k+1\).

4.2.2 Unitary mappings

Definition. A mapping \(U : H \to H'\) is unitary if

  1. \(U\) is linear, that is,

    \[U(\alpha f + \beta g) = \alpha U(f) + \beta U(g) \text{ for all } \alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{C} \text{ and } f, g \in H.\]

  2. \(U\) is bijection.

  3. \(\vert \vert Uf\vert \vert _{H'} = \vert \vert f\vert \vert _H\) for all \(f \in H\).

If such a map exists, we say that \(H\) and \(H'\) are unitary equivalent or unitary isomorphic.

Remark.

If \(U\) is unitary, then

  1. \(U^{-1}\) is also unitary.

  2. \((Uf, Ug)_{H'} = (f, g)_H\) for all \(f, g \in H\). Indeed, we observe that

    \[(F, G) = \frac{1}{4} \left[\vert \vert F + G\vert \vert ^2 - \vert \vert F - G\vert \vert ^2 + i\left(\vert \vert \frac{F}{i} + G \vert \vert ^2 - \vert \vert \frac{F}{i} - G \vert \vert ^2\right)\right].\]

Corollary 2.5.

Any two infinite dimensional Hilbert spaces are unitary equivalent.

Proof. Let \(\{e_1, e_2, \dots\} \subset H\) and \(\{e_1', e_2', \dots\} \subset H'\) be orthonormal basis respectively. We define

\[U : H \to H'\]

as follows: if

\[f = \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k e_k \quad \text{ then } \quad U(f) = g \text{ where } g \coloneq \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k e_k'.\]

Clearly, \(U\) is linear and bijection. Moreover, by Parseval’s identity,

\[\vert \vert Uf\vert \vert _{H'}^2 = \vert \vert g\vert \vert _{H'}^2 = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \vert a_k\vert ^2 = \vert \vert f\vert \vert _H^2.\]

Corollary 2.6.

\(H\) and \(H'\) are unitary equivalent if and only if they have the same dimension.

Example.

  1. Finite dimension \(H \approx \mathbb{C}^d\) or \(\mathbb{R}^d\)

  2. Infinite dimension \(H \approx l^2(\mathbb{N})\) or \(l^2(\mathbb{Z})\).

4.2.3 Pre-Hilbert spaces

Definition. A separable inner product space is called a Pre-Hilbert space.

Remark.

  1. \(H\) is called the completion of pre-Hilbert space \(H_0\).

  2. It is unique up to isomorphism. (See Exercise 14).

Proposition 2.7.

Let \(H_0\) be a pre-Hilbert space with \((\cdot, \cdot)_0\). Then there exists a Hilbert space \(H\) with \((\cdot, \cdot)_H\) such that

  1. \(H_0 \subset H\).

  2. \((f, g)_0 = (f, g)_H\) for all \(f, g \in H_0\).

  3. \(H_0\) is dense in \(H\).

Sketch of proof.

Consider the collection of Cauchy sequence

\[\{f_n\} \subset H_0.\]

Define an equivalence relation

\[\{f_n\} \sim \{f_n'\} \iff f_n - f_n' \to 0 \text{ as } n \to \infty.\]

Let \(H\) be the collection of equivalent classes and define

\[(f, g) = \lim_{n \to \infty} (f_n, g_n)_0\]

where \(\{f_n\}\) and \(\{g_n\}\) are Cauchy sequence representing \(f, g \in H\), respectively.<div class="real-analysis-footnote" markdown="1">Note: Please try to check well-definedness of the inner product!</div>

  1. \(H_0 \subset H\).
    If \(f \in H_0\), the constant sequence \(\{f\}\) is the corresponding element in \(H\).

  2. \((f, g) = (f, g)_0\) for all \(f, g \in H_0\) \(\to\) Clear!

  3. \(H_0\) is dense in \(H\). (Exercise!)

To prove \(H\) is complete<div class="real-analysis-footnote" markdown="1">Note: Separability of \(H\) is left as an exercise!</div>, let \(\{F^k\}\) be Cauchy in \(H\). Each \(F^k\) is represented by a Cauchy sequence

\[F^k = \{f_n^k\}_n \subset H_0\]

Define \(F \in H\) by the sequence \(\{f_n\}\) with \(f_n = f_{N(n)}^n\) where \(N(n)\) is chosen so that

\[\vert f_{N(n)}^n - f_j^n\vert < \frac{1}{n} \quad \forall \; j \ge N(n).\]

Then \(F^k \to F\) in \(H\).

Exercise: 4, 7, 14.

entry.title: Real Analysis 12: The Hilbert Space L2

link.title: Real Analysis 12: The Hilbert Space L2

entry.content:
이 글은 2026년 봄학기 실변수함수론(MAT4033) 강의노트를 주제별로 정리한 글입니다.

\(L^2\) space.

  1. The space \(L^2\) of square integrable functions is defined by

    \[L^2 \coloneq L^2(\mathbb{R}^d) \coloneq \left\{f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{C} \text{ measurable} : \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \vert f\vert ^2 < \infty \right\}\]

    where \(\vert f\vert ^2 = f\overline{f}\).

  2. The \(L^2\)-norm of \(f\) is defined by

    \[\vert \vert f\vert \vert _2 \coloneq \vert \vert f\vert \vert _{L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)} = \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \vert f\vert ^2\right)^{1/2}\]

  3. The \(L^2\)-inner product of \(f\) and \(g\) is defined by

    \[(f, g) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f \overline{g}\]

Remark.

  1. \(\vert \vert f\vert \vert _2 = 0\) if and only if \(f = 0\) a.e. Therefore, \(L^2\) is in fact the space of equivalence classes.

  2. \((f, f)^{1/2} = \vert \vert f\vert \vert _2\)

  3. \(\vert \vert \cdot\vert \vert _2\) is a norm and \((\cdot, \cdot)\) is an inner product by the following proposition.

Proposition 1.1.

  1. \(L^2\) is a vector space.

  2. (Cauchy-Schwarz inequality) If \(f, g \in L^2\), then \(f\overline{g}\) is integrable and

    \[\vert (f, g)\vert \le \vert \vert f\vert \vert _2 \vert \vert g\vert \vert _2\]

  3. For \(g \in L^2\), the map \(f \mapsto (f, g)\) is linear. Also, \((f, g) = \overline{(g, f)}\).

  4. (The triangle inequality)

    \[\vert \vert f + g\vert \vert _2 \le \vert \vert f\vert \vert _2 + \vert \vert g\vert \vert _2\]

Proof.

  1. Clear.

  2. Clearly,

    \[\int \vert f\overline{g}\vert \le \frac{1}{2}\int (\vert f\vert ^2 + \vert g\vert ^2) < \infty.\]

    1. If \(\vert \vert f\vert \vert _2 = 0\) or \(\vert \vert g\vert \vert _2 = 0\), then \(f\overline{g} = 0\) a.e. Thus \((f, g) = 0\).

    2. If \(\vert \vert f\vert \vert _2 = \vert \vert g\vert \vert _2 = 1\), then \(\vert (f, g)\vert \le \int \vert f\overline{g}\vert \le 1\).

    3. Suppose now that \(\vert \vert f\vert \vert _2 \neq 0\) and \(\vert \vert g\vert \vert _2 \neq 0\). Then

      \[\tilde{f} = \frac{f}{\vert \vert f\vert \vert _2} \quad \text{and} \quad \tilde{g} = \frac{g}{\vert \vert g\vert \vert _2}\]

      satisfy \(\vert \vert \tilde{f}\vert \vert _2 = \vert \vert \tilde{g}\vert \vert _2 = 1\).

    Hence, \(\vert (\tilde{f}, \tilde{g})\vert \le 1\). Then, \(\vert (f, g)\vert \le \vert \vert f\vert \vert _2 \vert \vert g\vert \vert _2\).

  3. Clear.

  4. By (ii) \& (iii),

    \[\begin{aligned} \vert \vert f + g\vert \vert _2^2 &= (f + g, f + g) \\ &= \vert \vert f\vert \vert _2^2 + (f, g) + (g, f) + \vert \vert g\vert \vert _2^2 \\ &\le \vert \vert f\vert \vert _2^2 + 2\vert \vert f\vert \vert _2 \vert \vert g\vert \vert _2 + \vert \vert g\vert \vert _2^2 \\ &= (\vert \vert f\vert \vert _2 + \vert \vert g\vert \vert _2)^2. \end{aligned}\]

Note that \(L^2\)-norm induces a metric \(d(f, g) = \vert \vert f - g\vert \vert _2\). Thus since we have metric on \(L^2\) space, then we can do the geometry in \(L^2\) space. Moreover, we can talk about the convergence in \(L^2\) space. In particular, we will see that \(L^2\) is complete and separable.

Theorem 1.2.

\(L^2\) is complete.

Proof. Let \(\{f_n\}\) be Cauchy in \(L^2\). We choose a subsequence \(\{f_{n_k}\}\) of \(\{f_n\}\) such that

\[\vert \vert f_{n_{k+1}} - f_{n_k}\vert \vert _2 < 2^{-k} \quad \forall \; k \ge 1.\]

Let

\[\begin{aligned} f &= f_{n_1} + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (f_{n_{k+1}} - f_{n_k}) \text{ and } \\ g &= \vert f_{n_1}\vert + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \vert f_{n_{k+1}} - f_{n_k}\vert \end{aligned}\]

and denote by \(S_K(f)\) and \(S_K(g)\) their partial sums. Then

\[\begin{aligned} \vert \vert S_K(g)\vert \vert _2 &\le \vert \vert f_{n_1}\vert \vert _2 + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \vert \vert f_{n_{k+1}} - f_{n_k}\vert \vert _2 \\ &< \vert \vert f_{n_1}\vert \vert _2 + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 2^{-k} < \infty. \end{aligned}\]

By the MCT, letting \(K \to \infty\) shows that \(\vert \vert g\vert \vert _2 < \infty.\)

Since \(\vert f\vert \le g\), we also have \(f \in L^2\). In particular, \(g < \infty\) a.e., and hence the series defining \(f\) converges a.e. Thus,

\[S_{K-1}(f) = f_{n_K} \to f \quad \text{a.e.}\]

Moreover, since

\[\vert f - S_K(f)\vert \le (2g)^2 \quad \text{for all } K \in \mathbb{N},\]

it follows from the DCT that

\[f_{n_k} \to f \quad \text{in } L^2.\]

Finally, recall that \(\{f_n\}\) is Cauchy. So for all \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) such that

\[\vert \vert f_n - f_m\vert \vert _2 < \frac{\epsilon}{2} \quad \forall \; n, m \ge N.\]

Choose \(k\) so that \(n_k > N\). Then

\[\vert \vert f_n - f\vert \vert _2 \le \vert \vert f_n - f_{n_k}\vert \vert _2 + \vert \vert f_{n_k} - f\vert \vert _2 < \epsilon \quad \forall \; n > N.\]

Theorem 1.3.

\(L^2\) is separable. i.e. there exists a countable dense subset of \(L^2\).

Proof. We claim that

\[\text{span} \{r\chi_R : R \text{ is rectangle with rational coordinates}\}\]

is dense in \(L^2\). Let \(f \in L^2\) and \(\epsilon > 0\). Consider

\[g_n(x) = \begin{cases} f(x) & \text{if } \vert x\vert \le n \text{ or } \vert f(x)\vert \le n \ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

Then

\[\vert f - g_n\vert \le (2\vert f\vert )^2 \quad \text{and} \quad g_n \to f \text{ a.e.}\]

Thus, by DCT, there exists \(N\) such that

\[\vert \vert f - g_N\vert \vert _2 < \frac{\epsilon}{2}.\]

Let \(g \coloneq g_N \in L^1\). Therefore, there exists a step function \(\varphi\) such that

\[\int \vert g - \varphi\vert < \frac{\epsilon^2}{16N}\]

We may also find a step function \(\psi\) with coefficients in \(\mathbb{Q} \times i\mathbb{Q}\) and rectangles with rational coordinates, such that

\[\vert \psi\vert \le N \quad \text{ and } \quad \int \vert g - \psi\vert < \frac{\epsilon^2}{8N}\]

Note that

\[\int \vert g - \psi\vert ^2 \le 2N \int \vert g - \psi\vert < \frac{\epsilon^2}{4} = \left(\frac{\epsilon}{2}\right)^2.\]

Consequently,

\[\vert \vert f - \psi\vert \vert _2 \le \vert \vert f - g\vert \vert _2 + \vert \vert g - \psi\vert \vert _2 < \epsilon.\]

Exercise: 5.

entry.title: Real Analysis 11: Rectifiable Curves
entry.content:
이 글은 2026년 봄학기 실변수함수론(MAT4033) 강의노트를 주제별로 정리한 글입니다.

Recall that a parametrized curve \(\gamma(t) = (x(t), y(t)) \in C[a,b]\) is rectifiable if and only if \(x, y \in BV[a,b]\). In this case, the length of \(\gamma(t)\) is defined by \(L \coloneq \sup_P \sum_{j=1}^N \vert z(t_j) - z(t_{j-1})\vert .\)

Question.

\(L = \int_a^b \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2} dt\)?

Answer.

No! If \(x = y = F =\) Cantor-Lebesgue function, which is continuous and of bounded variation, then \(\gamma\) is the straight line from \((0,0)\) to \((1,1)\) and has length \(\sqrt{2}\), but \(x' = y' = F' = 0\) almost everywhere.

Theorem 4.1.

If \(x\) and \(y\) are absolutely continuous, then \(\gamma\) is rectifiable and \(L = \int_a^b \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2} dt.\)

Proposition 4.2.

If \(F : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}\) is absolutely continuous, then \(T_F(a,b) \coloneq \int_a^b \vert F'(t)\vert dt.\)

Proof. (\(\ge\)) By Theorem 3.11 (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus), we have for any partition \(\mathcal{P}\),

\[\begin{aligned} \sum_{j=1}^N \vert F(t_j) - F(t_{j-1})\vert &= \sum_{j=1}^N \left\vert \int_{t_{j-1}}^{t_j} F'(t) dt \right\vert \\ &\le \sum_{j=1}^N \int_{t_{j-1}}^{t_j} \vert F'(t)\vert dt \\ &= \int_a^b \vert F'(t)\vert dt. \end{aligned}\]

Taking the supremum over \(\mathcal{P}\) gives the desired result.

(\(\le\)) This inequality is straightforward if \(G\) is absolutely continuous and \(G'\) is a step function: indeed, if \(G'\) is constant on each interval \((t_{j-1}, t_j)\), \(j=1,\dots,N\), then

\[\begin{aligned} T_G(a,b) &\ge \sum_{j=1}^N \vert G(t_j) - G(t_{j-1})\vert \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^N \left\vert \int_{t_{j-1}}^{t_j} G'(t) dt \right\vert \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^N \int_{t_{j-1}}^{t_j} \vert G'(t)\vert dt \\ &= \int_a^b \vert G'(t)\vert dt. \end{aligned}\]

Now, for the general case, we recall that step functions are dense in \(L^1\). Since \(F' \in L^1\), for any \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists a step function \(g\) such that \(\vert \vert F' - g\vert \vert _{L^1} < \epsilon.\) Let \(h = F' - g\) and define

\[G(x) = \int_a^x g(t) dt \quad \text { and } \quad H(x) = \int_a^x h(t) dt\]

Then, \(F = G + H\). Since

\[T_F \ge T_G - T_H \quad \text{and} \quad T_H \le \int_a^b \vert h\vert < \epsilon,\]

we have

\[\begin{aligned} T_F &\ge \int_a^b \vert g(t)\vert dt - \epsilon \\ &\ge \int_a^b \vert F'(t)\vert dt - 2\epsilon. \end{aligned}\]

Letting \(\epsilon \to 0\) yields the desired result.

Arc-length parametrization

For a rectifiable curve \(\gamma : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^2\), let \(L(A,B)\), \(a \le A \le B \le b\), denote the length function.

  • We define arc-length \(S : [a,b] \to [0, L] \text{ by } S(t) = L(a,t).\)

  • The arc-length parameterization of \(\gamma\) is \(\tilde{z}(s) = \tilde{x}(s) + i\tilde{y}(s) \text{ where }\tilde{z}(s) = z(t), s = S(t).\)

Theorem 4.3.

\(\tilde{x}, \tilde{y}\) are absolutely continuous, \(\vert \tilde{z}'(s)\vert = 1\) for almost everywhere \(s \in [0, L]\), and \(L = \int_0^L \sqrt{\tilde{x}'(s)^2 + \tilde{y}'(s)^2} ds.\)

Proof. Note that

\[\vert \tilde{z}(s_1) - \tilde{z}(s_2)\vert \le \vert s_1 - s_2\vert \quad \text{for all } s_1, s_2 \in [0, L].\]

Thus, \(\tilde{z}\) is absolutely continuous and \(\vert \tilde{z}'\vert \le 1\) almost everywhere. Moreover, by Theorem 4.2, \(L = \int_0^L \vert \tilde{z}'(s)\vert ds\). This completes the proof.

entry.title: Real Analysis 10: Functions of Bounded Variation and Absolute Continuity

link.title: Real Analysis 10: Functions of Bounded Variation and Absolute Continuity

entry.content:
이 글은 2026년 봄학기 실변수함수론(MAT4033) 강의노트를 주제별로 정리한 글입니다.

Main Question 2.

What conditions on \(F\) guarantee that \(F'\) exists a.e., that \(F' \in L^1\) and that

\[F(b) - F(a) = \int_a^b F'(x) dx.\]

cf. See Exercise 12: \(F' otin L^1\) in general.

3.3.1 Functions of bounded variation

Let \(\gamma\) be a parametrized curve in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) given by a continuous function,

\[z(t) = (x(t), y(t)), \quad t \in [a, b]\]

Definition. \(\gamma\) is rectifiable if there exists \(M < \infty\) such that for any partition \(P\),

\[P : a = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_N = b\]

the following holds:

\[\sum_{j=1}^N \vert z(t_j) - z(t_{j-1})\vert \le M.\]

The length of \(\gamma\) is defined by

\[L(\gamma) \coloneq \sup_P \sum_{j=1}^N \vert z(t_j) - z(t_{j-1})\vert = \inf M\]

Question.

What conditions on \(x, y\) guarantee rectifiability of \(\gamma\)?

Definition. A function \(F : [a,b] o \mathbb{C}\)

Note: \(F\) is not necessarily continuous.</div>is of bounded variation if there exists \(M < \infty\) such that for all partition of \([a,b]\),

\[\sum_{j=1}^N \vert F(t_j) - F(t_{j-1})\vert \le M.\]

We call \(\sum_{j=1}^N \vert F(t_j) - F(t_{j-1})\vert\) the variation of \(F\) with respect to \(P\). Furthermore, we define the set of all functions of bounded variation by

\[BV[a,b] := \{F : [a,b] o \mathbb{C} : F ext{ is of bounded variation}\}.\]

Theorem 3.1.

A curve parametrized by \((x(t), y(t)), a \le t \le b\), is rectifiable if and only if \(x\) and \(y\) are of bounded variation.

Proof. One may write \(F(t) = x(t) + iy(t)\). Observe that

\[F(t_j) - F(t_{j-1}) = (x(t_j) - x(t_{j-1})) + i(y(t_j) - y(t_{j-1})).\]

The results follows from \(\vert a + ib\vert \le \vert a\vert + \vert b\vert \le 2\vert a + ib\vert\).

Example.

  1. If \(F : [a,b] o \mathbb{R}\) is increasing and bounded, then \(F \in BV\) since

    \[\sum_{j=1}^N \vert F(t_j) - F(t_{j-1})\vert = F(b) - F(a) < 2 \sup \vert F\vert < \infty.\]

  2. If \(F\) is differentiable and \(F'\) is bounded, then \(F \in BV\). Indeed, by the MVT,

    \[\sum \vert F(t_j) - F(t_{j-1})\vert = \sum \vert F'(t_j^*)\vert (t_j - t_{j-1}) \le M(b-a).\]

    See also exercise 23.

  3. Let

    \[F(x) = egin{cases} x^a \sin(x^{-b}) & 0 < x \le 1 \ 0 & x = 0 \end{cases}\]

    Then \(F \in BV[0,1]\) if and only if \(a > b\). (Exercise 11).

Definition.

  1. The total variation of \(F\) on \([a,x]\) is defined by

    \[T_F(a, x) \coloneq \sup_P \sum_{j=1}^N \vert F(t_j) - F(t_{j-1})\vert\]

    where \(P\) is a partition of \([a,x]\).

  2. The positive variation of \(F : [a, b] o \mathbb{R}\)

    \[P_F(a, x) \coloneq \sup_P \sum_{(+)} (F(t_j) - F(t_{j-1}))\]

    where \((+)\) denotes the set of indices \(j\) for which \(F(t_j) - F(t_{j-1}) \ge 0\).

  3. The negative variation of \(F : [a, b] o \mathbb{R}\)

    \[N_F(a, x) \coloneq \sup_P \sum_{(-)} -(F(t_j) - F(t_{j-1}))\]

    where \((-)\) denotes the set of indices \(j\) for which \(F(t_j) - F(t_{j-1}) < 0\).

Note that the total variation allows complex-valued functions, whereas the positive and negative varations are defined only for real-valued functions.

Lemma 3.2.

Let \(F \in BV[a,b]\) be real-valued function. Then for all \(x \in [a,b]\),

\[F(x) - F(a) = P_F(a, x) - N_F(a, x) \quad ext{and} \quad T_F(a, x) = P_F(a, x) + N_F(a, x).\]

Proof. For all \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists a partition \(P\) such that

\[P_F - \sum_{(+)} (F(t_j) - F(t_{j-1})) < \epsilon \quad @@REAL_ANALYSIS_MATH_24@@ \quad N_F - \sum_{(-)} -(F(t_j) - F(t_{j-1})) < \epsilon.\]

That is, \(P\) is a refinement of \(P_F\) and \(N_F\). Since

\[F(x) - F(a) = \sum_{(+)} (F(t_j) - F(t_{j-1})) - \sum_{(-)} -(F(t_j) - F(t_{j-1}))\]

we have

\[\vert F(x) - F(a) - (P_F - N_F)\vert < 2\epsilon \implies F(x) - F(a) = P_F(a, x) - N_F(a, x).\]

This proves the first equality.

To prove the second equality, note that (\(\le\)) is trivial. Hence for the other direction (\(\ge\)), we get the following estimate:

\[ egin{aligned} P_F + N_F &\le \sum_{(+)} + \sum_{(-)} + 2\epsilon \ &= \sum_{j=1}^N \vert \cdot\vert + 2\epsilon \le T_F + 2\epsilon \implies P_F + N_F \le T_F \end{aligned}\]

This completes the proof.

Theorem 3.3.

Let \(F : [a,b] o \mathbb{R}\). Then \(F \in BV\) if and only if \(F\) is the difference of two increasing bounded functions.

Proof. (\(\impliedby\)) Clear.
(\(\implies\)) Write \(F(x) = (P_F(a, x) + F(a)) - N_F(a, x)\).

Remark.

Bounded variation is not necessariliy continuous.

Theorem 3.4.

If \(F \in BV[a,b]\), then \(F'\) exists a.e.

Lemma 3.5 (Rising sun).

Let \(G \in C(\mathbb{R})\). Let

\[E = \{x : G(x+h_x) > G(x) ext{ for some } h_x > 0\}.\]

If \(E eq \emptyset\), then \(E\) is open, hence \(E\) is countable union of open intervals

\[E = igcup_k (a_k, b_k).\]

Moreover, if \((a_k, b_k)\) is finite interval in this union, then \(G(a_k) = G(b_k)\).

Proof. If \(x \in E\), then there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that

\[G(y + h_x) > G(y) \quad orall \; y \in (x-\delta, x+\delta).\]

Thus, \(E\) is open. Now, consider \((a_k, b_k) \subset E\). Since \(a_k otin E\), \(G(b_k) \le G(a_k)\).

Suppose \(G(b_k) < G(a_k)\). By the MVT, there exists \(c \in (a_k, b_k)\) such that

\[G(c) = rac{1}{2}(G(a_k) + G(b_k))\]

We may choose \(c\) farthest to the right in \((a_k, b_k)\). Since \(c \in E\),

\[\exists \; d > c \quad ext{ such that } \quad G(d) > G(c)\]

Note that \(G(x) \le G(b_k)\) for all \(x \ge b_k\). So \(d < b_k\). Therefore, we can find \(c'\) as

\[c' \in (c, d) \subset (a_k, b_k) \quad ext{ such that } \quad G(c') = G(c)\]

by using MVT again. Which is contradiction to the choice of \(c\).

Corollary 3.6.

Lem 3.5 also holds for \(G \in C[a,b]\) and

\[E = \{x \in (a,b) : G(x+h_x) > G(x) ext{ for some } h_x > 0\}\]

except possibly when \(a = a_k\), in which case

\[G(a_k) \le G(b_k), \quad b = b_k, \quad ext{and} \quad G(a_k) \ge G(b_k).\]

Proof of Theorem 3.4.

  1. We assume \(F\) is increasing, bounded and continuous. We define

    \[ egin{aligned} D^+ F(x) &= \limsup_{0 < \pm h o 0} \Delta_h F(x) \quad ext{and}\ D_+ F(x) &= \liminf_{0 < \pm h o 0} \Delta_h F(x) \end{aligned}\]

    where \(\Delta_h F(x) = rac{F(x+h) - F(x)}{h}\). Then, it is enough to show that

    1. \(D^+ F < \infty\) a.e.

    2. \(D^+ F \le D_- F\) a.e.

    Indeed, (ii) applied to \(-F(-x)\) shows that

    \[D^- F \le D_+ F \quad ext{a.e.}\]

    and hence

    \[D^+ F \le D_- F \le D^- F \le D_+ F \le D^+ F < \infty \quad ext{a.e.}\]

    Now prove (i). Since

    \[\{D^+ F = \infty\} \subset \{D^+ F > \gamma\} \eqcolon E_\gamma \quad orall \; \gamma > 0,\]

    hence it suffices to show that<div class="real-analysis-footnote" markdown="1">Note: See Exercise 14 to show that \(E_\gamma \in \mathcal{M}\).</div>

    \[ ext{ETS : } m(E_\gamma) o 0 \quad ext{as } \gamma o \infty.\]

    We apply Corollary 3.6 to \(G(x) = F(x) - \gamma x\) :

    \[E_\gamma = igcup_k (a_k, b_k) \quad ext{ where } \quad F(b_k) - F(a_k) \ge \gamma (b_k - a_k).\]

    Then,

    \[ egin{aligned} m(E_\gamma) &= \sum_k m((a_k, b_k)) \ &\le \sum_k rac{1}{\gamma} (F(b_k) - F(a_k)) \ &\le rac{1}{\gamma} (F(b) - F(a)) o 0 \quad ext{as } \gamma o \infty. \end{aligned}\]

    Now, we prove (ii). Note that

    \[(a, b) \supset \{D^+ F > D_- F\} \subset igcup_{\overset{R, r \in \mathbb{Q}}{R > r}} \{D^+ F > R ext{ and } D_- F < r\}\]

    Then,

    \[ ext{ETS : } m(E) = 0 ext{ for fixed } R, r \in \mathbb{Q} ext{ with } R > r.\]

    Suppose \(m(E) > 0\). Then there exists an open \(\mathcal{O}\) such that

    \[E \subset \mathcal{O} \subset (a,b) \quad ext{and} \quad m(\mathcal{O}) < m(E) + rac{R}{r}.\]

    Write \(\mathcal{O} = igcup_n I_n\) with \(I_n\) disjoint intervals. We then have

    \[m(E) = \sum_n m(E \cap I_n) \quad ext{and} \quad rac{r}{R} \sum_n m(I_n) = rac{r}{R} m(\mathcal{O}) < m(E)\]

    Applying Corollary 3.6 to \(G(x) \coloneq F(x) - rx\) on for each \(I_n\), we have

    \[\{x \in I_n : G(x+h_x) > G(x) ext{ for some } h_x > 0\} = igcup_k (a_{k}, b_{k})\]

    and \(G(a_k) \ge G(b_k)\), that is

    \[F(b_k) - F(a_k) \le r (b_k - a_k)\]

    Applying Corollary 3.6 once again to \(H(x) \coloneq F(x) - Rx\) on each \((a_k, b_k)\), we have

    \[\{x \in I_n : H(x+h_x) > H(x) ext{ for some } h_x > 0\} = igcup_j (a_{k,j}, b_{k,j})\]

    and \(H(a_{k,j}) \ge H(b_{k,j})\), that is

    \[F(b_{k,j}) - F(a_{k,j}) \ge R (b_{k,j} - a_{k,j}).\]

    Let

    \[\mathcal{O}_n = igcup_{k,j} (a_{k,j}, b_{k,j}) \subset I_n.\]

    Since \(F\) is increasing,

    \[ egin{aligned} m(\mathcal{O}_n) = \sum_{k,j} (b_{k, j} - a_{k, j}) &\le \sum_{k,j} rac{1}{R} (F(b_{k,j}) - F(a_{k,j})) \ &\le rac{1}{R} \sum_k (F(b_k) - F(a_k)) \ &\le rac{1}{R} \sum_k r (b_k - a_k) \ &\le rac{r}{R} m(I_n). \end{aligned}\]

    Now, it suffices to show that

    \[E \cap I_n \subset \mathcal{O}_n.\]

    In fact, if \(y \in E \cap I_n\), then \(D_- F(y) < r\), and hence

    \[\exists \; h < 0 ext{ such that } rac{F(y+h) - F(y)}{h} < r,\]

    that is, \(G(y+h) > G(y)\). Thus,

    \[y \in (a_k, b_k) ext{ for some } k.\]

    Also, \(D^+ F(y) > R\) implies that there exists \( ilde{h} > 0\) such that

    \[ rac{F(y+ ilde{h}) - F(y)}{ ilde{h}} > R\]

    that is, \(H(y+ ilde{h}) > H(y)\). Thus,

    \[y \in (a_{k,j}, b_{k,j}) ext{ for some } j.\]

  2. For general case, we will prove this theorem at Section 3.3.

Corollary 3.7.

\(F : [a,b] o \mathbb{R}\). If \(F\) is increasing and continuous, then \(F'\) exists a.e.. Moreover, \(F'\) is measurable, nonnegative, \(F' \in L^1[a,b]\) and

\[\int_a^b F'(x) dx \le F(b) - F(a)\]

In particular, if \(F\) is bounded on \(\mathbb{R}\), then \(F' \in L^1(\mathbb{R})\).

Proof. Since

\[G_n(x) \coloneq rac{F(x + rac{1}{n}) - F(x)}{ rac{1}{n}} o F'(x) \quad ext{a.e.}\]

by Theorem 3.4, \(F'\) is measurable and nonnegative. We may assume \(F \in C(\mathbb{R})\). By Fatou’s lemma,

\[\int_a^b F' dx \le \liminf_{n o \infty} \int_a^b G_n\]

But,

\[ egin{aligned} \int_a^b G_n &= rac{1}{1 / n} \int_a^b F(x + rac{1}{n}) dx - rac{1}{1 / n} \int_a^b F(x) dx \ &= rac{1}{1 / n} \int_{a + rac{1}{n}}^{b+ rac{1}{n}} F(x) dx - rac{1}{1 / n} \int_a^b F(x) dx \ &= \mathop{ lap{-}\int}_{b}^{b + rac{1}{n}} F(x) dx - \mathop{ lap{-}\int}_{a}^{a + rac{1}{n}} F(x) dx o F(b) - F(a) \quad ext{as } n o \infty. \end{aligned}\]

The Cantor-Lebesgue function

We construct an increasing function

\[F \in C[0,1] ext{ with } F(0)=0, F(1)=1 ext{ but } F' = 0 ext{ a.e.}\]

so that so that \(\int_0^1 F' eq F(1) - F(0)\). Let \(C = igcap_k C_k\) be the Cantor set. Then \(\{F_n\}\) is sequence of increasing functions in \(C[0,1]\) such that

\[\vert F_{n+1} - F_n\vert < 2^{-n-1} \quad ext{on } [0,1]\]

Thus, \(F_n ightrightarrows F \in C[0,1]\). Note that \(F\) is increasing, \(F(0)=0\), \(F(1)=1\), and \(F\) is constant on each interval of \([0,1] \setminus C\). Since \(m(C)=0\), \(F' = 0\) a.e.

3.3.2. Absolutely continuous functions

Definition. \(F : [a,b] o \mathbb{R}\) is called absolutely continuous if for all \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that

\[\sum_{k=1}^N \vert F(b_k) - F(a_k)\vert < \epsilon\]

whenever

\[\sum_{k=1}^N (b_k - a_k) < \delta ext{ for disjoint intervals } (a_k, b_k),\]

Remark.

  1. Absolutely continuous \(\implies\) uniformly continuous \(\implies\) continuous.

  2. \(AC \subset BV[a,b]\).

  3. If \(f \in L^1\), then

    \[F(x) = \int_a^x f(y) dy\]

    is absolutely continuous by Proposition 1.12 in Chapter 2. This implies absolutely continuous is a necessary condition for \(\int_a^b F' = F(b) - F(a)\).

    Note: If \(\int_a^b F' = F(b) - F(a)\), then \(\int_a^x F' = F(x) - F(a)\) for all \(x \in [a,b]\), which implies \(F(x) = \int_a^x F' + F(a)\) is absolutely continuous.</div>

    </li> </ol>

    Theorem 3.8.

    If \(F\) is absolutely continuous on \([a,b]\), then \(F'\) exists almost everywhere. Moreover, if \(F' = 0\) almost everywhere, then \(F\) is constant.

    Definition. Let \(E \subset \mathbb{R}^d\). A collection \(\mathcal{B}\) of balls is a Vitali covering of \(E\) if for all \(x \in E\) and \(\eta > 0\), there exists \(B \in \mathcal{B}\) such that \(x \in B\) and \(m(B) < \eta\).

    Following Lemma 3.9 suggests that we can find a finitely many disjoint balls from Vitali covering with error \(\delta\), which cover almost of \(E\).

    Lemma 3.9.

    Let \(\mathcal{B}\) be a Vitali covering of \(E\), where \(m(E) < \infty\). Then for all \(\delta > 0\), there exists finitely many disjoint balls \(B_1, \dots, B_N \in \mathcal{B}\) such that

    \[\sum_{i=1}^N m(B_i) > m(E) - \delta.\]

    Proof. We may assume \(\delta < m(E)\).

    Note: If \(\delta \ge m(E)\), then \(m(E) - \delta \le 0\)</div> Take a compact subset \(E'\) of \(E\) with \(m(E') \ge \delta\), and cover \(E'\) by finitely many balls from \(\mathcal{B}\). By Vitali’s covering argument, we can select a disjoint subcollection \(\{B_1, \dots, B_{N_1}\} \subset \mathcal{B}\) such that

    \[\sum_{i=1}^{N_1} m(B_i) \ge 3^{-d} m(E') \ge 3^{-d} \delta.\]

    Note that first inequality comes from Lemma 1.2. If the left-hand side \(\sum_{i=1}^{N_1} m(B_i) > m(E) - \delta\), then we are done.

    Otherwise, that is, \(\sum_{i=1}^{N_1} m(B_i) < m(E) - \delta\), we have \(m(E_2) > \delta\), where

    \[E_2 = E \setminus igcup_{i=1}^{N_1} \overline{B_i}\]

    Since \(\sum_{i=1}^{N_1} m(B_i) < m(E) - \delta \implies \delta < m(E) - \sum_{i=1}^{N_1} m(B_i) = m(E_2)\) Note that the balls in \(\mathcal{B}\) that are disjoint from \( igcup_{i=1}^{N_1} \overline{B_i}\) still cover \(E_2\):

    If \(x \in E_2\), then \( ext{dist}(x, igcup_{i=1}^{N_1} \overline{B_i}) > 0.\) Thus, for all \(\eta > 0\), there exists \(B \in \mathcal{B}\) such that \(x \in B\), \(m(B) < \eta\) and \(B \cap B_i = \emptyset\). In fact, this gives a Vitali covering for \(E_2\).

    We repeat the previous argument and choose a disjoint subcollection \(\{B_{N_1+1}, \dots, B_{N_2}\} \subset \mathcal{B}\) such that

    \[\sum_{i=N_1+1}^{N_2} m(B_i) \ge 2 \cdot 3^{-d} \delta.\]

    Continuing this way, we would have selected a collection of disjoint balls \(\{B_1, \dots, B_{N_k}\} \subset \mathcal{B}\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^{N_k} m(B_i) \ge k \cdot 3^{-d} \delta\) at the \(k\)-th stage. Thus, this process must stop after finite steps.

    Corollary 3.10.

    We can arrange the choice of balls such that \(m(E \setminus igcup_{i=1}^N B_i) < 2\delta.\)

    Proof. Let \(\mathcal{O} \supset E\) be open with \(m(\mathcal{O} \setminus E) < \delta\). Then, we can restrict all of our choices above to balls contained in \(\mathcal{O}\). Since \((E \setminus igcup B_i) \cup igcup B_i = E \subset \mathcal{O},\) we have

    \[ egin{aligned} m(E \setminus igcup B_i) &\le m(\mathcal{O}) - m( igcup B_i) \ &\le m(E) + \delta - (m(E) - \delta) \ &= 2\delta. \end{aligned}\]

    Proof of Theorem 3.8.

    It is enough to show that \(F(a) = F(b)\).

    Let \(E = \{x \in (a,b) : F'(x) ext{ exists and is zero}\}\). Then \(m(E) = b - a\). Fix \(\epsilon > 0\). By the absolute continuity of \(F\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that

    \[\sum_{k=1}^M \vert F(b_k) - F(a_k)\vert < \epsilon\]

    whenever

    \[\sum_{k=1}^M (b_k - a_k) < \delta ext{ for disjoint intervals } (a_k, b_k).\]

    Now, we construct a Vitali covering of \(E\) as follows: Let \(x \in E\) and \(\eta > 0\). Since

    \[\lim_{h o 0} \vert rac{F(x+h) - F(x)}{h}\vert = 0\]

    there exists an open interval \((a_x, b_x) \subset [a,b]\) such that \(x \in (a_x, b_x)\), \(b_x - a_x < \eta\), and

    \[\vert F(b_x) - F(a_x)\vert \le \epsilon(b_x - a_x).\]

    The collection of these intervals forms a Vitali covering of \(E\). By Lemma 3.9, there exists finitely many disjoint \(I_i = (a_i, b_i)\), \(1 \le i \le N\) such that

    \[\sum_{i=1}^N m(I_i) > m(E) - \delta = b - a - \delta.\]

    This implies that \([a,b] \setminus igcup_{i=1}^N I_i = igcup_{k=1}^M [a_k, b_k]\) has measure \(m( igcup_{k=1}^M [a_k, b_k]) \le \delta\), and hence

    \[\sum_{k=1}^M \vert F(b_k) - F(a_k)\vert < \epsilon.\]

    Therefore,

    \[ egin{aligned} \vert F(b) - F(a)\vert &\le \sum_{i=1}^N \vert F(b_i) - F(a_i)\vert + \sum_{k=1}^M \vert F(b_k) - F(a_k)\vert \ &\le \epsilon \sum_{i=1}^N (b_i - a_i) + \epsilon \ &\le \epsilon(b - a) + \epsilon, \end{aligned}\]

    which shows \(F(b) - F(a) = 0\).

    Following Theorem 3.11, answers our last remaining main question 2.

    Theorem 3.11.

    Suppose \(F\) is absolutely continuous on \([a,b]\). Then, \(F' \in L^1[a,b]\) and

    \[F(x) - F(a) = \int_a^x F'(y) dy \quad ext{for all } x \in [a,b].\]

    Conversely, if \(f \in L^1[a,b]\), then \(F(x) = \int_a^x f(y) dy\) is absolutely continuous and \(F' = f\) almost everywhere.

    Proof. Since \(F\) is the difference of two continuous increasing functions, Corollary 3.7 shows that \(F' \in L^1[a,b].\)

    Define \(G(x) = \int_a^x F'(y) dy\). Then, by the Lebesgue’s differentiation theorem,

    \[G' = F' ext{ a.e.}\]

    Since \(G - F\) is absolutely continuous, it follows from Theorem 3.8 that \(G - F\) is constant. Therefore, \(G(x) - F(x) = G(a) - F(a) \implies F(x) - F(a) = \int_a^x F'\).

    3.3.3 Differentiability of jump functions

    Lemma 3.12.

    A bounded increasing function \(F : [a,b] o \mathbb{R}\) has at most countably many discontinuities.

    Proof. If \(F\) is discontinuous at \(x\), then

    \[ ext{there exists } r_x \in \mathbb{Q} ext{ such that } F(x^-) < r_x < F(x^+).\]

    Moreover, if \(F\) is discontinuous at \(x < z\), then \(r_x < F(x^+) \le F(z^-) < r_z.\)

    Let \(\{x_n\}\) be the set of discontinuities of a bounded increasing function \(F\). Let \(\alpha_n = F(x_n^+) - F(x_n^-).\) Then \(F(x_n^+) = F(x_n^-) + \alpha_n\) and \(F(x_n) = F(x_n^-) + heta_n \alpha_n\) for some \( heta_n \in [0,1]\). Define

    \[j_n(x) = egin{cases} 0 & ext{if } x < x_n \ heta_n & ext{if } x = x_n \ 1 & ext{if } x > x_n \end{cases}\]

    and the jump function associated to \(F\) by \(J(x) \coloneq J_F(x) \coloneq \sum_{n=1}^\infty \alpha_n j_n(x).\)

    Lemma 3.13.

    If \(F\) is bounded and increasing on \([a,b]\), then

    1. \(J\) is discontinuous precisely at \(\{x_n\}\) and has a jump at \(x_n\) equal to that of \(F\).

    2. \(F - J\) is increasing and continuous.

    Proof.

    1. If \(x eq x_n\) for all \(n\), then \(J\) is the uniform limit of functions continuous at \(x\). If \(x = x_N\) for some \(N \in \mathbb{N}\), then \(\sum_{n eq N} \alpha_n j_n\) is continuous at \(x\) and \(\alpha_N j_N\) has a jump discontinuity at \(x_N\) of size \(\alpha_N\).

    2. Clearly, \(F - J\) is continuous. If \(x < y\), then

      \[ egin{aligned} J(y) - J(x) &\le \alpha_x (1 - heta_x) + \sum_{x < x_n < y} \alpha_n + \alpha_y heta_y \ &\le F(y) - F(x). \end{aligned}\]

      Note that \(\alpha_x, \alpha_y, heta_x, heta_y\) correspond to the jump at \(x\) and \(y\). They vanish if \(F\) is continuous at \(x\) and \(y\).

    Remark.

    Since \(F = (F - J) + J\), Theorem 3.4 follows from the following lemma.

    Lemma 3.14.

    \(J'\) exists and vanishes almost everywhere.

    Proof. Let \(\epsilon > 0\) and \(E = \left\{ x : \limsup_{h o 0} rac{J(x+h) - J(x)}{h} > \epsilon ight\} \in \mathcal{M}.\) It is enough to show that \(\delta \coloneq m(E) = 0.\)

    Let \(\eta > 0\). Since \(\sum \alpha_n < \infty\), there exists \(N\) such that \(\sum_{n > N} \alpha_n < \eta.\) We write \(J_0 = \sum_{n > N} \alpha_n j_n\), then \(J_0(b) - J_0(a) < \eta.\)

    Since \(J - J_0 = \sum_{n=1}^N \alpha_n j_n\) is a finite sum, the set \(E_0 = \left\{ x : \limsup_{h o 0} rac{J_0(x+h) - J_0(x)}{h} > \epsilon ight\}\) differs from \(E\) by at most a countable set \(\{x_1, \dots, x_N\}\). Thus, \(m(E_0) = \delta\).

    We take a compact subset \(K\) of \(E_0\) with \(m(K) \ge \delta / 2.\) For each \(x \in K\), we can find \((a_x, b_x) i x\) such that \(J_0(b_x) - J_0(a_x) > \epsilon(b_x - a_x).\) By compactness of \(K\) and Vitali’s covering argument, there exists disjoint \(I_j\),

    \[I_j = (a_j, b_j), \quad j=1,\dots,M ext{ such that } \sum_{j=1}^M m(I_j) > rac{m(K)}{3}.\]

    Now,

    \[ egin{aligned} J_0(b) - J_0(a) &\ge \sum_{j=1}^M (J_0(b_j) - J_0(a_j)) \ &> \epsilon \sum_{j=1}^M (b_j - a_j) \ &> rac{\epsilon}{3} m( K) \ge rac{\epsilon}{6} \delta. \end{aligned}\]

    This shows that \( rac{\epsilon}{6} \delta < \eta\). Since \(\eta > 0\) was arbitrary, we conclude \(\delta = 0\).

이 글은 2026년 봄학기 실변수함수론(MAT4033) 강의노트를 주제별로 정리한 글입니다.

Definition. A family \(\{K_\delta\}_{\delta > 0} \subset L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)\) is an approximation to the identity if

  1. \(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} K_\delta = 1 \quad \forall \delta > 0\),

  2. \(\vert K_\delta(x)\vert \le A \delta \min \left\{ \frac{1}{\delta^{d+1}}, \frac{1}{\vert x\vert ^{d+1}} \right\}\) for all \(\delta > 0\) and for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\).

Example.

  1. Let \(\varphi \ge 0\) be bounded, supported on \(\overline{B}_1\), and such that \(\int \varphi = 1\). Then,

    \[K_\delta(x) := \frac{1}{\delta^d} \varphi\left(\frac{x}{\delta}\right)\]

    is an approximation to the identity.

  2. The Poisson kernel, heat kernel, Fej'{e}r kernel, \dots See the textbook!

Before we seek to following theorem, recall that we have defined the convolution \(f * K_\delta\) by

\[(f * g)(x) \coloneq \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f(x-y)g(y)dy\]

Theorem 2.1.

If \(f \in L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)\), then

\[(f * K_\delta)(x) \to f(x) \quad \text{as } \delta \to 0\]

for every Lebesgue point \(x\). In particular, the limit holds a.e. <div class="real-analysis-footnote" markdown="1">Note: Note that \(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f(x-y)K_\delta(y)dy - \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f(x)K_\delta(y)dy = (f * K_\delta)(x) - f(x)\)</div>

To prove Theorem 2.1, we need the following lemma.

Lemma 2.2.

Let \(f \in L_{loc}^1\) and let \(x\) be a Lebesgue point of \(f\). Then,

\[r \mapsto A(r) := \frac{1}{r^d} \int_{\vert y\vert \le r} \vert f(x-y) - f(x)\vert dy\]

is continuous, bounded, and \(\lim_{r \to 0} A(r) = 0\).

Proof. Note that continuity of \(A\) follows from proposition 1.12 in Chapter 2, and \(\lim_{r \to 0} A(r) = 0\) follows from the definition of Lebesgue point. It remains to show that \(A\) is bounded on \((1, \infty)\). That is,

\[\text{ETS : } A \text{ is bounded on } (1, \infty).\]

If \(r > 1\), then

\[\begin{aligned} A(r) &\le \frac{1}{r^d} \int_{\vert y\vert \le r} \vert f(x-y)\vert dy + \vert B_1\vert \vert f(x)\vert \\ &\le \vert \vert f\vert \vert _{L^1} + \vert B_1\vert \vert f(x)\vert < \infty \end{aligned}\]

Note: Calculation of \(\frac{1}{r^d} \int_{\vert y\vert \le r} \vert f(x)\vert dy\) is given by \(\frac{1}{r^d} \int_{\vert y\vert \le r} \vert f(x)\vert dy = \frac{1}{r^d} \vert B_r\vert \vert f(x)\vert = \vert B_1\vert \vert f(x)\vert\)</div>

Proof of Theorem 2.1.

We write

\[\begin{aligned} \vert (f * K_\delta)(x) - f(x)\vert &\le \int \vert f(x-y) - f(x)\vert \vert K_\delta(y)\vert dy \\ &\le \int_{\vert y\vert \le \delta} \vert f(x-y) - f(x)\vert \frac{c}{\delta^d} dy \\ &+ \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \int_{2^k \delta < \vert y\vert \le 2^{k+1}\delta} \vert f(x-y) - f(x)\vert \frac{c\delta}{(2^k \delta)^{d+1}} dy \\ &\lesssim A(\delta) + \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2^k} A(2^{k+1}\delta) \qquad (\ast) \end{aligned}\]

Note: If \(k=0 : \delta < \vert y\vert \le 2\delta, \quad k=1 : 2\delta < \vert y\vert \le 4\delta\)</div>

Let \(\epsilon > 0\). Then there exists \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) such that

\[\sum_{k=N}^{\infty} 2^{-k} < \epsilon\]

By Lemma 2.2, there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that

\[A(2^k \delta) < \frac{\epsilon}{N} \quad \text{for } k = 0, 1, \dots, N-1.\]

Recalling that \(A\) is bounded, we have

\[(\ast) \le \frac{\epsilon}{N} + \frac{\epsilon}{N} \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \frac{1}{2^k} + C \epsilon \lesssim \epsilon\]

Theorem 2.3.

If \(f \in L^1\), then \(f * K_\delta \in L^1\) and

\[\vert \vert f * K_\delta - f\vert \vert _{L^1} \to 0 \quad \text{as } \delta \to 0.\]

Proof. Homework.
